evidence.observation: The single apply path for a Gateway session update. For every scanned row it calls upsertSyncedUserSession (line 163) and increments the changed/inserted/updated counters only inside `if (result.changed)` (lines 164-168). A replayed identical update therefore returns changed:false and contributes zero to every counter, so a duplicate event cannot be counted twice; a distinct event still increments exactly once.

Deterministic field normalization (sessionKey, agentId, channel, peer, label, lastActivity) with stable fallbacks. Because the same raw Gateway row always normalizes to an identical object, a replay reaches the upsert with byte-identical fields, which is what lets the downstream change comparison conclude 'unchanged' instead of re-writing state.

Second guard against duplicate events above the upsert layer: a per-user cooldown (line 190) and an in-flight promise map (lines 195-199, 214) that returns the existing promise for a concurrent replay. Two simultaneous replays of the same update therefore produce one Gateway call and one state change, not two.
Clears the inFlightByUserId and lastSyncAtByUserId module maps so the duplicate-event fixture starts from a clean scheduler state and its coalescing assertion is not polluted by earlier runs.

The idempotency authority the contract rests on. On an existing row it computes `changed` by comparing agent/channel/peer/label/display_title/tenant/last_message_at (updated_at is deliberately excluded) and returns { changed: false, action: 'unchanged' } with no UPDATE when nothing differs; last_message_at uses Math.max so replaying an older or equal timestamp never advances state.

Usage is written through _persistOwnerScopedUpdate as an absolute SET of token_*/msg_*/cost_total columns, not a read-modify-write increment, so re-applying the same usage payload is a no-op on the totals and cannot double-count. This is the usage-side half of the duplicate-event contract.

claims.claim: Replaying one identical Gateway session update cannot emit a duplicate state change: syncUserSessionsFromGateway only counts and persists when upsertSyncedUserSession reports result.changed, and the upsert reports changed:false for an identical row, so a replayed event yields changed=0 while a distinct event yields changed=1.

Replaying one session update cannot double-count usage: usage columns are persisted as absolute values by the owner-scoped UPDATE, so applying the same update twice leaves token/msg/cost totals identical rather than summing them, and the sync counters (changed/inserted/updated) are likewise not re-incremented on replay.

Duplicate delivery is suppressed at two layers: deterministic normalization makes a replay field-identical, the upsert then rejects it as 'unchanged', and scheduleUserSessionSync additionally coalesces concurrent replays for the same user into a single in-flight sync via cooldown plus the inFlightByUserId promise map.

conclusion: The duplicate-event contract holds. Executing the real server/core/session-sync.js against a distinct duplicate-event fixture (one Gateway session update delivered twice, plus a concurrent scheduled replay) produced exactly one state change and one usage application for the first delivery, zero for the verbatim replay, and still applied a genuinely newer update exactly once. The two independent guards (unchanged-detection in upsertSyncedUserSession and in-flight coalescing in scheduleUserSessionSync) mean a replayed event can neither double-count usage nor emit a duplicate state change. A negative control with dedup disabled makes the fixture fail, confirming the assertions have teeth.
